strengths: Conditional summary graphs are a useful contribution: under the assumption that outgoing effects depend on the source variable’s state, K graphs compactly represent K^N joint state configurations. This meaningfully extends approaches based on a single global regime.

The combination of shared interaction functions, amortized graph inference, and state-dependent message passing is well motivated. The paper clearly explains its relationship to NRI/ACD and distinguishes population identifiability from the unresolved consistency of its learning procedure.

The synthetic results demonstrate benefits within the proposed setting. For example, Table 2 reports 97.08% summary-graph accuracy versus ACD’s 60.45% for two edge types with hidden states. Experiments varying state counts, training-set sizes, and numbers of variables, together with NBA forecasting, provide useful breadth.
weaknesses: The central identifiability guarantee needs a more precise statement and proof. Theorem 1 omits the nonconstant-mechanism assumption used in Lemma 2. More importantly, Appendix A.3 invokes causal minimality to conclude dependence after conditioning on all other lagged variables, whereas minimality directly guarantees dependence only conditional on the other parents. That implication requires additional justification and suitable support/nondegeneracy assumptions. The result also concerns population identification, rather than recovery by the proposed VAE.

The comparisons do not adequately establish an advantage over methods designed for switching causal structures. Regime-PCMCI is identified as closely related but is not evaluated; most evaluated baselines assume fixed structures or smoothly changing mechanisms. Moreover, SDCI learns shared dynamics from 50,000 training sequences, while several competitors fit individual sequences. Comparisons with switching-regime methods and amortized dynamic-graph models are needed to isolate the proposed contribution.

The demonstrated hidden-state capability is substantially narrower than the introductory framing suggests. Appendix F.2 explicitly reports unsuccessful causal recovery with hidden history-dependent states and supplies state supervision for scenario class 3. Successful hidden-state experiments mainly use simple deterministic functions of current observations. This limitation should appear prominently in the main text. Performance also deteriorates substantially in the unrestricted three-edge-type setting, where Table 2 does not show a clear advantage over TdCM.

The graph-recovery evaluation is incomplete for the central claim about changing structures. In particular, the hidden-state spring comparison reports accuracy of the union summary graph, which discards when edges occur and can be dominated by edge prevalence. Actual graph densities, trivial prediction baselines, precision/recall, and quantitative conditional or full-time graph recovery would make these results more convincing.

NBA forecasting improvements support the usefulness of the model’s inductive bias, but do not establish that its learned interactions are causal. A comparable state-conditioned graph predictor without causal-structure discovery would help assess that interpretation. The rollout protocol also needs clarification about access to future ball features and state labels, and the train/test construction should establish separation between games and potentially overlapping events.

Reproduction and uncertainty assessment remain incomplete despite the implementation appendix. The manuscript does not clearly specify the graph-prior probabilities, hidden-state network architecture, latent-label alignment for accuracy calculations, or the number of training runs and meaning of the reported error bars. The unexplained lambda parameter in Appendix C.2 further obscures the training objective.
